<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">As neural network model sizes have dramatically increased, so has the interest in various techniques to reduce their parameter counts and accelerate their execution. An active area of research in this field is sparsity – encouraging zero values in parameters that can then be discarded from storage or computations. While most research focuses on high levels of sparsity, there are challenges in universally maintaining model accuracy as well as achieving significant speedups over modern matrix-math hardware. To make sparsity adoption practical, the NVIDIA Ampere GPU architecture introduces sparsity support in its matrix-math units, Tensor Cores. We present the design and behavior of Sparse Tensor Cores, which exploit a 2:4 (50%) sparsity pattern that leads to twice the math throughput of dense matrix units. We also describe a simple workflow for training networks that both satisfy 2:4 sparsity
pattern requirements </span><span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">and</span><span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> maintain accuracy, verifying it on a wide range of common tasks and model architectures. This workflow makes it easy to prepare accurate models for efficient deployment on Sparse Tensor Cores.</span></p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">In the area of Deep Learning, using larger neural network models typically leads to higher accuracy for various tasks </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a><span id="S1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
Modern state-of-the-art models can consist of hundreds of billions of parameters and require trillions of compute operations per input sample.
Pruning of neural network parameters has emerged as an important technique to reduce model sizes and compute requirements at inference time.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Pruning accomplishes this by pushing certain parameter values to zero, inducing sparsity in a model </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a><span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
However, existing pruning methods can struggle to simultaneously maintain model accuracy and gain inference performance (speed).
Fine-grained sparsity maintains accuracy but poorly utilizes memory accesses and fails to take advantage of modern vector and matrix math pipelines, thus it does not outperform traditional dense models on processor architectures such as GPUs.
Coarse-grained sparsity can better utilize processor resources but fails to maintain accuracy beyond moderate sparsity ratios.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">In this paper, we describe a 2:4 (read as “two-to-four”) sparsity pattern that halves a model’s parameter count, requiring that every group of consecutive four values contains at least two zeros.
We also describe a workflow to prune traditional, dense models for this pattern while maintaining their accuracy.
This workflow prunes weights of a densely-trained model once, then repeats the training session with a fixed sparsity pattern using the same hyper-parameters as in the original training session.
Furthermore, we describe Sparse Tensor Cores, introduced in the NVIDIA Ampere GPU architecture </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a><span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, to accelerate operations on 2:4 sparse matrices.
Sparse Tensor Cores double math throughput for matrix-multiply operations when the first argument is a compressed 2:4 sparse matrix.
Matrix multiplication is a compute primitive behind math-intensive neural network operations such as convolutions, linear layers, recurrent cells, and transformer blocks.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The contributions of this paper include: (1) a fine-grained 2:4 structured pruning approach, (2) a compression format to efficiently store such pruned tensors in memory, (3) hardware architecture to accelerate sparse matrix multiplication involving a 2:4 sparse tensor, and (4) an empirically-verified workflow that re-trains pruned weights to eliminate accuracy loss in many standard networks.
We summarize prior sparsity research in Section </span><a href="#S2" title="2 Related Work ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a><span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
The 2:4 pattern, compressed storage format required by Sparse Tensor Cores, and Sparse Tensor Core operation are detailed in Section </span><a href="#S3" title="3 Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a><span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
Section </span><a href="#S4" title="4 Network Pruning Workflow ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a><span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> describes the methodology for training neural networks to have 2:4 weight sparsity so that inference can be accelerated.
In Section </span><a href="#S5" title="5 Results ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a><span id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, we provide an empirical study on a variety of popular tasks and neural network architectures highlighting the universality of our proposed workflow in maintaining model accuracy while not having to change any hyper-parameters.
Section </span><a href="#S6" title="6 Conclusions and Future Work ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a><span id="S1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> concludes the paper with a summary and directions for future work.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Neural network model pruning approaches can be grouped into the following categories:</span></p>
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">train and prune a dense model, then fine-tune the remaining weights in the model to recover accuracy,</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">train a dense model with gradual pruning to obtain a sparse model,</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">train a sparse model with a sparsity pattern selected </span><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">a priori</span><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, or</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">train a sparse model with a sparsity pattern determined based on trained dense version.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fine-tuning methods prune fully-trained dense weights and continue to fine-tune
the remaining weights for additional training samples.
Different approaches in this space can be distinguished by the pruning method, pruning schedule, sparsity structure, and fine-tuning schedule used during the fine-tuning phase.
Pruning methods typically eliminate weights using weight magnitude based metrics </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a><span id="S2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
or some salience-based criteria </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a><span id="S2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">).
A variety of pruning schedules have been proposed – single step </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a><span id="S2.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> and
gradual/iterative </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a><span id="S2.p2.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.13" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. Iterative methods prune weights gradually over a number of steps, in each step eliminating either a fixed number of weights </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.14" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a><span id="S2.p2.1.15" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.16" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> or choosing a fraction of weights based on an analytical function </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.17" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a><span id="S2.p2.1.18" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.19" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. Furthermore, the pattern used to prune models may adhere to a specific structure </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.20" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a><span id="S2.p2.1.21" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.22" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
or follow no structure at all </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.23" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a><span id="S2.p2.1.24" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.25" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. Structured pruning removes parameters in groups (entire filters, channels, etc.) in order to exploit hardware and software optimized for dense computation. However, at higher levels of sparsity these pruning methods lose model accuracy </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.26" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a><span id="S2.p2.1.27" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.28" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. For example, ResNet-50 can see a 2</span><math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S2.p2.1.29" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> speedup through channel pruning, but close to 1.5%
accuracy is lost </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.30" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a><span id="S2.p2.1.31" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.32" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. Unstructured pruning eliminates individual parameters without any regard to the resulting pattern. Networks pruned with unstructured sparsity tend to retain more accuracy than similarly sized networks pruned with structured sparsity, but they rarely fully utilize the underlying hardware capabilities. For example, model parameters can be pruned by
nearly 13</span><math id="S2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S2.p2.1.33" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> with no loss in accuracy, but the pruning pattern is not
conducive to hardware acceleration </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.34" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a><span id="S2.p2.1.35" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.36" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. Hence, the performance
benefit with such unstructured pruning approaches is negligible and at times
negative, even when pruning rate is
high (e.g. 95%) </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.37" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a><span id="S2.p2.1.38" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.39" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
The difficulty of getting inference speed benefits with unstructured patterns is even more pronounced on processor architectures with matrix pipelines, such as GPUs and TPUs (Tensor Cores and systolic arrays,
respectively). No universal fine-tuning schedule has been proposed yet – schedules often vary from model to model (for example,using 10 epochs of fine-tuning for one network but requiring 20 epochs for another network model</span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p2.1.40" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a><span id="S2.p2.1.41" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p2.1.42" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">).</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Some approaches train models with a fixed sparsity pattern starting from the random initialization of the network, but the pattern is computed based on a fully trained </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a><span id="S2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> or partially trained </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a><span id="S2.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> dense model of the same architecture. These approaches maintain accuracy and achieve 80%-99% sparsity. While run-time is not discussed in these works, given the use of unstructured sparsity, it is unlikely for these pruned models to efficiently utilize modern matrix processors.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Sparse models can also be obtained by starting from randomly-initialized dense models and gradually introducing sparsity as training progresses </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a><span id="S2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. Typically, 70%-99% unstructured sparsity is targeted to prepare models for inference. As described above, these models struggle to outperform dense models due to their unstructured sparsity. Furthermore, to maintain accuracy, model and training hyper-parameters are often modified, and these modifications can be quite model-specific. For example, in </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a><span id="S2.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">,
the hidden size of a recurrent network was increased by 1.75</span><math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S2.p4.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> while pruning to 95% sparsity. In another case </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p4.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a><span id="S2.p4.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p4.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, the training schedule was extended for some networks by 5</span><math id="S2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S2.p4.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> in order to reach the same accuracy as the dense model.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Finally, there have been proposals to design sparse model architectures, aimed at efficient hardware utilization during training and inference. Most prominent example of this category is block sparsity, where sparsity is introduced at a block level allowing good utilization of matrix math pipelines </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a><span id="S2.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. However, similar to approaches discussed above, in order to maintain accuracy, one has to increase the hidden size compared to the dense model. Block sparsity has found use for cases where using a larger hidden size enables higher accuracy but is impractical with dense models.
Additionally, there has been work investigating fine-grained structured sparsity and motivating the need to prune in a fine-grained pattern that is conducive to hardware acceleration </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a><span id="S2.p5.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p5.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
Key points are optimized GPU kernels to speed up such pruned models on CUDA cores </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p5.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a><span id="S2.p5.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p5.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> and the benefits of custom hardware to speed up structurally pruned models </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S2.p5.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a><span id="S2.p5.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S2.p5.1.13" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.</span></p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection" style="font-size:90%;">Summary:</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS0.SSSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">While a variety of approaches for pruning neural networks to high degrees of sparsity have been proposed, no one method has been described to maintain accuracy while achieving inference speedup.
Fine-tuning workflows provide inconclusive results on which pruning schemes to use (e.g. magnitude or heuristic based weight pruning, prune partially trained or fully trained weights), what pruning method to follow (e.g. one-shot or iterative pruning, layer by layer pruning or whole network pruning.) and what fine-tuning schedule to use (e.g. how many epochs of fine-tuning, what learning rate to use, etc.). In short, extracting performance from hardware by pruning networks while maintaining accuracy and using a fine-tuning workflow that is consistent across a variety of networks is still an open problem.
This motivated our search for a sparsity pattern that enables hardware acceleration as well as maintains accuracy with a workflow applicable over a wide range of neural network tasks and models.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We introduce 2:4 sparsity to address the challenges of adopting sparsity outlined in the last section. The 2:4 pattern mandates that for each group of 4 values, at least 2 must be zero. This leads to 50% sparsity, which makes maintaining accuracy without hyper-parameter exploration much more practical than, say, 80% sparsity. When applied to a matrix, the 2:4 pattern has the following benefits over alternative sparsity approaches:</span></p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:0.45in;">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">efficient memory accesses</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">a low-overhead compressed format</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">2x math throughput increase on the NVIDIA Ampere GPU architecture</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S3.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The pattern and compressed format are detailed in Section </span><a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 2:4 Sparsity and Its Benefits ‣ 3 Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a><span id="S3.p1.2.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, while Sparse Tensor Cores that take advantage of this format are described in Section </span><a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Structured-Sparse GEMM on Tensor Cores ‣ 3 Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a><span id="S3.p1.2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2104.08378v1/fig_compressed_matrix-storage.svg" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:357/180;" width="357" height="180"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Structured-sparse matrix (W) storage format. The uncompressed matrix is of dimension R <math id="S3.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> C and the compressed matrix is of dimension R <math id="S3.F1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="S3.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{C}{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{C}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> .</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>2:4 Sparsity and Its Benefits</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An example of a matrix that satisfies 2:4 sparsity pattern requirement is shown in Figure </span><a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
With this pattern, only the 2 nonzero values in each group of 4 values need to be stored.
Metadata to decode compressed format is stored separately, using 2-bits to encode the position of each nonzero value within the group of 4 values.
For example, metadata for the first row of matrix in Figure </span><a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> is </span><math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[[0,3],[1,2]]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">[</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">[</mo><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">0</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">3</mn></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">]</mo></mrow><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">[</mo><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">1</mn><mo mathsize="0.900em">,</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">]</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[[0,3],[1,2]]</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
Metadata information is needed to fetch corresponding values from the second matrix when performing matrix multiplication.
Note that for a group of 4 values having more than 2 zeros, the compressed format will still store 2 values to maintain a consistent format.</span></p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection" style="font-size:90%;">Efficient memory accesses:</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Unstructured sparsity patterns lead to poor utilization of cache lines when accessing memory, thus under utilizing memory bandwidth. Furthermore, unstructured patterns commonly use CSR/CSC/COO storage formats </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S3.SS1.SSSx1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a><span id="S3.SS1.SSSx1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S3.SS1.SSSx1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, which lead to data-dependent accesses, thereby increasing latency for matrix reads.
In contrast, 2:4 sparsity has the same level of sparsity at every sub-block of the larger matrix, which enables hardware to fully-utilize large memory reads.
Similarly, since the sparsity is constant across the matrix, there is no indirection required; a nonzero value’s position in memory can be determined from the compression rate directly.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection" style="font-size:90%;">Compressed format efficiency:</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Using CSR format for unstructured sparsity can introduce storage overhead due to metadata of up to 200% (consider 8b quantized weight values for inference: column-index for the value would require 16-bits or more for even modestly-sized matrices). Due to its 4-value block size, the 2:4 sparse storage format (shown in Figure </span><a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a><span id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">) requires only 2-bits metadata per value, limiting storage overhead to 12.5% and 25% for 16b and 8b values, respectively. For 16-bit operands, storing a sparse tensor in compressed format leads to </span><math id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">44% savings in storage capacity:
4 dense elements require 4</span><math id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ast" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">∗</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ast</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">16 = 64-bits of storage while 2:4 sparsity leads to 2</span><math id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ast" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">∗</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ast</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">16-bits + 2</span><math id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ast" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">∗</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ast</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">2-bits = 36-bits to store the two non-zero elements. For 8-bit operands, storing in compressed format saves </span><math id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">38% in memory capacity and bandwidth compared to the dense tensor.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Structured-Sparse GEMM on Tensor Cores</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Tensor Cores, first introduced in the NVIDIA Volta GPU architecture, accelerate matrix-multiply-and-accumulate (MMA) instructions that are fundamental to neural network layers involving math operations such as convolutions, linear layers, recurrent cells, and transformer blocks.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2104.08378v1/fig_dense_sparse_gemm.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:464/244;" width="464" height="244" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>
Mapping a M<math id="S3.F2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>N<math id="S3.F2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>K GEMM onto a Tensor Core.
Dense matrix <math id="S3.F2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>, of size M<math id="S3.F2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>K, (left side) becomes M<math id="S3.F2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times\frac{K}{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mfrac><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times\frac{K}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (right side) after pruning with 2:4 sparsity.
Sparse Tensor Core hardware selects only the elements from B that correspond to the nonzero values in A, skipping the unnecessary multiplications by zero.
In both dense and sparse GEMMs, B and C are dense K<math id="S3.F2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>N and M<math id="S3.F2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>N matrices, respectively.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>A100 Tensor Core input/output formats (numeric precision)
and performance in tera-operations per second (TOPS).</figcaption>

<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S3.T1.4.3" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S3.T1.4.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.3.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">156</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.4.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.3.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">312</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.4.4" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S3.T1.4.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">FP16</span></th>
<th id="S3.T1.4.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">FP32</span></th>
<td id="S3.T1.4.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.4.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">312</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.4.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.4.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">624</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.4.5" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S3.T1.4.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">BF16</span></th>
<th id="S3.T1.4.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">FP32</span></th>
<td id="S3.T1.4.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.5.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">312</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.4.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.5.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">624</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.4.6" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S3.T1.4.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">FP16</span></th>
<th id="S3.T1.4.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">FP16</span></th>
<td id="S3.T1.4.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.6.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">312</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.4.6.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.6.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">624</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.4.7" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S3.T1.4.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.7.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">INT8</span></th>
<th id="S3.T1.4.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.7.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">INT32</span></th>
<td id="S3.T1.4.7.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.7.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">624</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.4.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S3.T1.4.7.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1248</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The NVIDIA Ampere GPU architecture extends the Tensor Cores to also handle 2:4 sparsity by allowing the first argument be stored in the sparse format described in Section </span><a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 2:4 Sparsity and Its Benefits ‣ 3 Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
Thus, Sparse Tensor Cores perform sparse matrix </span><math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> dense matrix = dense matrix operation (the second input matrix and the output matrix are dense).
Figure </span><a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Structured-Sparse GEMM on Tensor Cores ‣ 3 Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> shows how a 2:4 sparse GEMM operation is mapped to Tensor Cores.
50% sparsity on one of the operands halves the required multiply-and-add operations, resulting in (up to) a 2</span><math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> performance increase over equivalent dense GEMMs. Sparse Tensor Cores support FP16, BF16, and 8b-integer input/output types. Furthermore, TF32 mode is supported for FP32 input/output but the pattern becomes 1:2 sparse. Peak dense and sparse Tensor Core throughputs are shown in Table </span><a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Structured-Sparse GEMM on Tensor Cores ‣ 3 Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">It is the application’s responsibility to ensure that the first operand is a matrix stored in the compressed 2:4 format. cuSPARSELt and other libraries provide APIs for compression and sparse math operations, while, starting in version 8.0, the TensorRT SDK performs these functions for 2:4 sparse weights automatically. NVIDIA libraries require that input dimensions of a sparse matrix multiplication be multiples of 16 and 32 for 16-bit (FP16/BF16) and 8b-integer formats, respectively.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Speedups that 2:4 sparse matrix multiplications achieve over dense multiplications depend on several factors, such as arithmetic intensity and GEMM dimensions.
Figure </span><a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Structured-Sparse GEMM on Tensor Cores ‣ 3 Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> shows speedups achieved over a sampling of GEMM dimensions (cuSPARSELt</span><span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cusparselt/index.html</span></span></span><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> cuBLAS</span><span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
            https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/index.html</span></span></span><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> libraries were used for the sparse and dense GEMMs, respectively).
As larger GEMMs tend to have higher arithmetic intensity, they get closer to the </span><math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" mathsize="0.900em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> speedup afforded by Sparse Tensor Cores.
For language modeling networks, N is often the sequence length times the batch size: for a sequence length of 256, one would need a batch size of 40 to see this plot with N equal to 10K.
M and K are related to the hidden dimensions of the layers in the network, which is typically scaled up to increase network accuracy; GPT-3 </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, for example, uses a hidden size of 12,288.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2104.08378v1/fig_gemmperf.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:357/154;" width="357" height="154"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Comparison of sparse and dense INT8 GEMMs on NVIDIA A100 Tensor Cores. Larger GEMMs
achieve nearly a 2<math id="S3.F3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup with Sparse Tensor Cores.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Network Pruning Workflow</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">In this section, we describe a workflow that prunes a network with the 2:4 sparsity pattern, maintains original accuracy, and avoids any hyper-parameter searches. Since our aim is to reduce neural network size and run-time at deployment, we trade a higher training cost for a simple and general workflow – the additional training cost can be amortized over the deployment lifetime of days to months.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2104.08378v1/fig_simple_recipe.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/145;" width="333" height="145"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>A typical network training process adapted for 2:4 sparsity: dense training (step 1) is followed by a pruning stage (step 2) and a second, identical training stage (step 3).</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>The Basic Workflow</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">While our proposed workflow trains a network twice, it achieves universality - as we will show, it can be applied across a wide range of neural network architectures and tasks. It follows the basic train, prune, and fine-tune approach:</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:0.45in;">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Train a model without sparsity,</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Prune the model in a 2:4 sparse pattern,</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Retrain the pruned model:</span></p>
<ul id="S4.I1.i3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">initialize the weights to the values from Step 2,</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">use the same optimizer and schedule (learning-rate, schedule, number of epochs, etc.) as in Step 1,</span></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">maintain the sparsity pattern computed in Step 2.</span></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">This workflow is implemented in the Automatic SParsity (ASP) </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> library for PyTorch and is illustrated in Figure </span><a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4 Network Pruning Workflow ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, where the two training stages are identical in learning rate schedule and length and are separated by the one-shot pruning step.
While Step 1 is straightforward, some details about Steps 2 and 3 follow.</span></p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection" style="font-size:90%;">Step 2: Weight pruning:</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">At its simplest, the pruning step removes the two smallest weights in each group of four to meet the 2:4 pattern requirement, as illustrated in Figure </span><a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Step 2: Weight pruning: ‣ 4.1 The Basic Workflow ‣ 4 Network Pruning Workflow ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. We found using the magnitude criteria sufficient, but one could consider other metrics, such as output activation similarity or instantaneous gradients.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2104.08378v1/fig_zeroing-matrix.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:357/160;" width="357" height="160"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Step 2 of the workflow modifies the weights in the dense matrix (W<sub id="S4.F5.6" class="ltx_sub">0</sub>) on the left to conform to the 2:4 constraint, yielding the sparse matrix (W) on the right.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2104.08378v1/fig_permute-matrix.svg" id="S4.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/195;" width="429" height="195"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Permuting columns of a weight matrix prior to pruning the matrix can reduce the effect of the 2:4 sparsity constraint on weight magnitude.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">At this point in the workflow, the opportunity exists to change the layout of the network’s weights using channel permutations to minimize the impact of the pruning step.
Figure </span><a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Step 2: Weight pruning: ‣ 4.1 The Basic Workflow ‣ 4 Network Pruning Workflow ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> shows how this works on a random dense matrix (top-left).
When this matrix is pruned with the 2:4 sparse constraint (top-right), some relatively large values are lost, resulting in a final total weight magnitude of 83.7.
By first permuting columns of this weight matrix to distribute the large values more evenly (lower-left), they are preserved after pruning (lower-right), for a final total weight magnitude of 102.9.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Since permutations are applied to columns of weights (the </span><math id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathsize="0.900em">A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> matrix in Figure </span><a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Structured-Sparse GEMM on Tensor Cores ‣ 3 Sparsity Support in the NVIDIA Ampere Architecture ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">), the rows of activations (</span><math id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathsize="0.900em">B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">) must be similarly permuted to maintain the same result for the GEMM operation.
We accomplish this by permuting the </span><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">rows</span><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> of the weights used to produce those activations, typically the weights of the previous layer.
For convolutions, permutations are applied to the input channel dimension, which becomes a component of the weight matrix’s column dimension.
This process does not change the computations performed or the network’s results and incurs no runtime overhead.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">For the majority of networks tested, these permutations are not required - step 2 is as simple as enforcing the 2:4 constraint on the weight tensors as they are.
However, some networks are designed with efficiency in mind and begin with very few parameters; simply pruning and fine-tuning these models may still result in accuracy loss.
Channel permutations make the most of each nonzero parameter and allow 2:4 sparsity to maintain accuracy for these parameter-efficient networks, as shown in Table </span><a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.1 Image Classification Networks ‣ 5 Results ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. Details about finding quality permutations will be presented separately.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection" style="font-size:90%;">Step 3: Sparse retraining:</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSSx2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We use retraining to recover model accuracy lost when half of the weights are removed by Step 2 of the workflow.
To avoid any hyper-parameter search, we simply repeat the training session from Step 1, starting with weights from Step 1 rather than a random initialization.
It is important to reset all hyper-parameters and optimizer state, such as momenta, etc.
Any weight removed in Step 2 should retain its zero value in order to maintain the 2:4 sparsity pattern.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Layers to Prune</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">In our studies, we prune only layers that have learnable parameters and lead to a GEMM-like operation during the neural network’s execution on hardware.
Such layers include convolution, fully-connected, and recurrent layers.
We do not prune layers with inner dimensions (GEMM-K for fully-connected or recurrent layers and C</span><math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">R</span><math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">S for convolution layers) that are not multiples of 16 and 32 for 16-bit floating point and 8b-integer formats, respectively.
We also do not prune embedding layers (typical in language processing tasks) since these layers effectively implement a lookup table.
Further, since our goal is to speed up inference, we do not prune layers that are involved only in the training phase and not in the inference phase of the network.
Such layers include language-modeling heads used during training in language processing networks (like BERT </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">) which are then replaced by task-specific heads during inference, auxiliary classifiers used in Inception networks </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> which are removed altogether for deployment, and the entirety of discriminator networks used in adversarial training of generative networks (GANs).</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Applying the Workflow to Models Trained in Multiple Phases</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">For models that are trained in a single phase, the application of the workflow from Section </span><a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 The Basic Workflow ‣ 4 Network Pruning Workflow ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> is straightforward.
Examples of single-phase training include image classification networks trained on the ILSVRC2012 </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> dataset, language translation networks trained on a single dataset, etc.
However, when networks are trained in multiple phases, we can consider how many and which phases to consider for Steps 1 and 3 of the workflow.
For example, object detection networks are often trained in 2 phases: first the backbone is trained on ILSVRC2012, then the detector heads are added and the model is trained for detection on COCO </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> dataset.
Another example is question answering networks, such as BERT, that are first trained for language modeling and </span><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">then</span><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> trained for question answering on another dataset.
We break such scenarios down into two categories:</span></p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection" style="font-size:90%;">Cases that require pruning and retraining the first phase:</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">In some cases where the second phase trains on a small data set, we have observed that the pruned network does not go through enough updates to recover accuracy after pruning if only the second phase is used for the retraining step of the workflow.
An example of this case is a language model like BERT, which is pre-trained on a very large dataset and then fine-tuned on a much smaller dataset for downstream tasks.
The solution to this problem is to simply prune and retrain after the </span><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">pre-training</span><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> step, as shown in Figure </span><a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Cases that require pruning and retraining the first phase: ‣ 4.3 Applying the Workflow to Models Trained in Multiple Phases ‣ 4 Network Pruning Workflow ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
Then, the fine-tuning for the downstream task starts with a sparse and retrained model and simply maintains the sparsity pattern.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2104.08378v1/fig_bert_recipe.svg" id="S4.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/124;" width="476" height="124"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>BERT’s downstream tasks are too small recover accuracy lost by pruning the language model, so the pre-training is repeated with sparsity before fine-tuning for the downstream task.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2104.08378v1/fig_detector_recipe.svg" id="S4.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:310/121;" width="310" height="121"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span>A detection network’s fine-tuning of the detection heads is enough to recover accuracy lost by pruning the backbone, so the pruning step is inserted after the full network is trained, and only the fine-tuning is repeated.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection" style="font-size:90%;">Cases that can prune and retrain only the second phase:</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">In contrast to language models, common object detection tasks fine-tune with a large-enough data set to </span><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">not</span><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> require repeating the backbone’s pre-training. In this case, it is sufficient to train a dense backbone and fine-tune detection or segmentation heads. At this point, after all the weights have been trained, they can be pruned and the fine-tuning repeated, as shown in Figure </span><a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ Cases that require pruning and retraining the first phase: ‣ 4.3 Applying the Workflow to Models Trained in Multiple Phases ‣ 4 Network Pruning Workflow ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. It is important to note that the task-specific heads have to be fine-tuned before they can be pruned.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSSx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSSx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSSx2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">These examples show different types of two-phase training; the same principles can be applied to training sessions consisting of more than two phases.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Combining Sparsity and Quantization</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Quantization is a popular technique to accelerate neural network inference – by adapting the network to use narrower integer types, for example INT8, we can both reduce memory bandwidth pressure and benefit from higher throughput math pipelines </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a><span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
Quantizing a network typically starts with a network trained in floating point, then calibration is applied to determine the parameters for replacing floating point values and math with low-bit integer ones.
While some networks retain accuracy immediately after quantization, others require fine-tuning to recover lost accuracy. For both types of networks our recommendation is to apply quantization calibration (and potentially fine-tuning) </span><span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">after</span><span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> a network has been pruned (and retrained) for sparsity.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">We evaluate the workflow proposed in Section </span><a href="#S4" title="4 Network Pruning Workflow ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a><span id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> across a range of problem domains, tasks, and neural network architectures. For training each of the networks, we use hyper-parameters and training details mentioned in the papers introducing the network architecture and/or popular public repositories of network implementations.
We examine model accuracy for both floating point networks as well as their quantization to INT8.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Top-1 accuracy of image classification networks evaluated on the ImageNet ILSVRC2012 dataset

<td id="S5.T2.4.9.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.45pt 10.0pt;"><span id="S5.T2.4.9.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">79.9</span></td>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Image Classification Networks</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Image classification networks are trained in a single phase, thus retraining simply repeats the training step schedule (with the exact same hyper-parameters and learning rate schedule as used to train the network) starting with the network initialized to its pruned trained weights.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table </span><a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5 Results ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> shows the accuracy of a wide variety of networks: popular networks like ResNet </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, VGG </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> and Inception </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, stacked U-Nets (SUNet) </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.13" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.14" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, dilated residual networks (DRN) </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.15" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.16" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.17" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
We also examine networks trained with weakly (WSL) or semi-weakly supervised learning (SWSL) methods </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.18" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.19" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.20" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> which use additional data to improve accuracy.
We prune all the convolution and fully-connected layers except for the first one (</span><math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="7\times 7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn mathsize="0.900em">7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" mathsize="0.900em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn mathsize="0.900em">7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">7\times 7</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.21" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> convolution on 3-channel input) since they do not have a GEMM-K dimension that is an even multiple of 16.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Small, parameter-efficient networks that struggle with the baseline fine-tuning approach match the target accuracy when permuting before fine-tuning (ILSVRC2012).</figcaption>
