</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Weight and input activation tensors in convolution layers, including the first layer, and fully-connected layers are quantized to INT8.
Entropy and max calibration </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> are used for activations and weights, respectively.
Per-tensor scaling factors are used for activation tensors, per-channel scaling factors are used for weight tensors in convolutions, and per-row scaling factors are used for weight tensors in fully-connected layers.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The results in Table </span><a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5 Results ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> indicate the accuracy is maintained for both floating point and quantized networks when sparsity workflow from Section </span><a href="#S4" title="4 Network Pruning Workflow ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> is applied.
While for some networks, sparse and quantized models accuracy is slightly different than for the dense non-quantized counterparts, these differences are within bounds of run-to-run variation caused by random seeds or fine-tuning non-determinism.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Some of the lower-parameter networks (MobileNet v2 </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, SqueezeNet </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, MNASNet </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, ShuffleNet v2 </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.13" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, and EfficientNet </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.14" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.15" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.16" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">) do not fully recover accuracy when applying the basic workflow.
As Table </span><a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.1 Image Classification Networks ‣ 5 Results ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a><span id="S5.SS1.p5.1.17" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> shows, permuting the weights before pruning allows a fully recovery of accuracy for these models.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Image Segmentation and Detection Networks</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">To study object detection and segmentation, we use networks from PyTorch Torchvision, Detectron2 </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, NVIDIA Deep Learning Examples for Tensor Cores </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, and NVIDIA ADLR </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> repositories.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Image segmentation and object detection models are typically trained in two phases: first a backbone is trained for image classification, followed by the addition of model components (segmentation/detection heads, FPN, etc.), and then training for detection or segmentation.
Backbones are trained on the ILSVRC2012 dataset, downstream tasks are trained on COCO 2017 </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, with some semantic segmentation networks also using Mapillary and Cityscapes datasets.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Since these detection and segmentation datasets are relatively large, we find that we can prune the weights after the second phase and repeat the training of only the second phase.
Accuracy results are summarized in Table </span><a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5.2 Image Segmentation and Detection Networks ‣ 5 Results ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a><span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, which shows sparse results matching those of the dense counterparts.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">For each network, all layers in the backbone (except the very first 3-channel convolution) and heads are pruned with 2:4 sparsity,
and all layers (including the first convolution) are quantized to INT8.
Similar to classification networks, entropy calibration with per-tensor scaling factors are used for activation tensors, and max calibration with per-channel or per-row scaling factors are used for weight tensors.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Accuracy of detection (bbox Average Precision, top) and image segmentation (mask Average Precision, bottom) networks with 2:4 sparsity on the COCO 2017 dataset.
In this table, RN=ResNet, FPN=Feature Pyramid Network, and RPN=Region Proposal Network.
1x and 3x are the length of fine-tuning schedules as referred to in Detectron2.
</figcaption>

<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">As part of devising a scheme for stabilizing the fine-tuning of sparse GANs </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a><span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, we apply the procedure from Section </span><a href="#S4" title="4 Network Pruning Workflow ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a><span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> to generate 2:4 sparse floating-point networks to a variety of GANs and tasks.
The results for Frechet Inception Distance (FID) scores </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a><span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> (lower is better) from this work are shown in Table </span><a href="#S5.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 5.2 Image Segmentation and Detection Networks ‣ 5 Results ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a><span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Networks for Natural Language Processing (NLP)</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">To study the behavior of our workflow on NLP tasks, we select recurrent-based translation network (GNMT </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">), Transformer-based translation network (FairSeq Transformer </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">), and two language modeling networks (Transformer-XL </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> and BERT </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.13" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">).</span></p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSSx1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection" style="font-size:90%;">Language Translation:</h4>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSSx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSSx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Language translation networks are trained in a single-phase, thus the training session is repeated using the original hyper-parameters after pruning.
After fine-tuning, the networks are
quantized to INT8 using max calibration </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">. Per-tensor scaling factors are used for activation tensors and per-row scaling factors are used for weight tensors in fully-connected and recurrent layers.
Table </span><a href="#S5.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Language Translation: ‣ 5.4 Networks for Natural Language Processing (NLP) ‣ 5 Results ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> shows the accuracy of networks retrained for the 2:4 pattern matching that of the dense originals.</span></p>
</div>

<td id="S5.T7.7.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:7.0pt;padding-right:7.0pt;"><span id="S5.T7.7.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Sparse</span></td>
<td id="S5.T7.7.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:7.0pt;padding-right:7.0pt;"><span id="S5.T7.7.2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Dense</span></td>
<td id="S5.T7.7.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:7.0pt;padding-right:7.0pt;"><span id="S5.T7.7.2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Sparse</span></td></tr>

</section>
<section id="S5.SS4.SSSx2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection" style="font-size:90%;">Language Modeling:</h4>

<div id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The Enwik8 </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> dataset is used for Transformer-XL evaluation, and SQuAD v1.1 </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> is used for BERT evaluation.
State-of-art language modeling networks involve a two-stage training process:
unsupervised training (also called pre-training) on large-scale unlabeled data sets, followed by fine-tuning on much smaller data sets for
downstream tasks, such as question-answering and entailment classification.
For these networks, our studies show that repeating pre-training step after pruning
and then fine-tuning the sparse network on target task
leads to a model that matches dense network’s accuracy (shown in Table </span><a href="#S5.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Language Translation: ‣ 5.4 Networks for Natural Language Processing (NLP) ‣ 5 Results ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">).
We use the BERT</span><sub id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.9" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">LARGE</span></sub><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> model and training scripts as described in NVIDIA Megatron repository </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p1.1.13" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">.
For both networks, all GEMM layers involving weight/parameter tensors inside a transformer block/layer are pruned (attention layers are not pruned since they do not involve any weights).</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">When quantizing BERT to INT8, all GEMM layers including batched-GEMM layers operate on INT8 operands, along with data in the residual connections.
This aggressive quantization can cause a small accuracy degradation, but sparsity matches the dense accuracy in both cases. Per-tensors scaling factors are used with max calibration for weight tensors and percentile calibration </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S5.SS4.SSSx2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> for activations tensors in fully-connected layers. The pruned pre-trained language model is fine-tuned for both quantization operations as well as the SQuAD dataset’s task-specific heads at the same time.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusions and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Sparsity in neural networks remains an active research area. Unstructured sparsity, which is the subject of many research efforts, requires very high levels of sparsity in order to achieve speedups over dense math on modern processors with matrix-math pipelines. However, very sparse networks have difficulty maintaining model accuracy. To overcome these challenges, we introduced 2:4 structured sparsity, hardware primitives for its acceleration, and a workflow for pruning networks. The NVIDIA Ampere GPU architecture introduces Sparse Tensor Cores, which have 2</span><math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo mathsize="0.900em">×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> math throughput for GEMM-like operations (convolutions and matrix multiplies) where the first argument is a tensor with 2:4 sparsity. The workflow was empirically shown to maintain accuracy over a wide range of tasks and neural network models, trained using standard learning rate schedules found in public code repositories.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The proposed sparsity workflow repeats a training session after pruning the weights of a trained dense networks. The benefit of this approach is that retraining does not require any hyper-parameter changes or searches. However, since this workflow doubles the training time, an interesting direction for future investigations is finding shorter fine-tuning schedules. Some preliminary experiments with a grid-search have identified a set of hyper-parameters (initial learning rate, learning rate schedule and epochs/iterations to fine-tune) for shorter fine-tuning sessions that maintained accuracy. However, these parameters were highly network- and task-dependent, and we have not yet been able to identify hyper-parameters that work universally for various tasks and networks. Thus, a universal approach to reduced fine-tuning requirements remains future work. Another interesting direction for future work is exploring the effects of sparsity on models that were trained to the limits of their capacity - there are indications that some popular models can achieve higher accuracy when trained on larger datasets or with longer training schedules. While we looked at some models trained on larger datasets (with weakly and semi-weakly supervised techniques) in Section </span><a href="#S5" title="5 Results ‣ Accelerating Sparse Deep Neural Networks" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a><span id="S6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, evaluating alternative training schedules is an interesting next step.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Our proposed workflow targets acceleration of inference. While this matches what would be needed to accelerate the forward pass of training, in order to also accelerate the backward pass of training, the 2:4 constraint must also be satisfied by the transposed weight tensors. This can be done by enforcing the constraint along both dimensions of the weight matrix: rows </span><span id="S6.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">and</span><span id="S6.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> columns. The PyTorch ASP </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S6.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a><span id="S6.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S6.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> library provides a simple greedy approach, as well as an exhaustive search, that seeks to minimize the weight magnitude lost by pruning; investigation of more efficient mask-finding algorithms is an active research area (for example, </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S6.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a><span id="S6.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S6.p3.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">) and is left as future work. To accelerate training, one would also aim to minimize the number of updates performed with a dense network. For this, one may need to train with dynamic sparsity masks, evolving them during training </span><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><span id="S6.p3.1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">[</span><a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a><span id="S6.p3.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">]</span></cite><span id="S6.p3.1.12" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> (as opposed to static masks computed once during pruning, which this paper shows to suffice for inference). Thus, investigation of dynamic mask requirements is an intriguing area for future work as well.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Finally, it is also interesting to investigate pruning of activations, as some layers, such as multi-head attention in Transformer-based networks, do not involve any weights. Our preliminary experiments suggest that it is possible to prune activations with a 2:4 pattern without accuracy loss; a fully general methodology is future work.</span></p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>

</span>
</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span id="bib.bib65.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Learning N:M fine-grained structured sparse neural networks from
scratch.
</span>
</span>
<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span id="bib.bib65.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">In </span><span id="bib.bib65.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">ICLR</span><span id="bib.bib65.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">, 2021.
</span>
</span></li>
    
</ul>
</section>
</article>
</div>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
